title: Biosphere to Ecosystems
seo_title: SSS 1 Biology: Biosphere to Ecosystems Worksheets (WAEC/NECO)
standard_text: The biosphere, biomes and ecosystems; abiotic factors (light, temperature, water, soil) and biotic factors; energy flow through food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids; nutrient cycles (carbon, water, nitrogen); Nigerian biomes. (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 1; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 1 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): interactions and niches, energy flow and food webs, energy flow and trophic levels, cycling of matter and ecological pyramids. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Energy flows through an ecosystem; nutrients are recycled.
key_sub: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.
body_html:
How to think about it

An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with each other and with abiotic factors such as light, water, temperature and soil. Nigeria's biomes include mangrove swamps and rainforest in the south, and Guinea, Sudan and Sahel savanna in the north.

Producers make food by photosynthesis; consumers eat other organisms; decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. At each trophic level energy is lost as heat in respiration, so food chains are short. Carbon, water and nitrogen are recycled.

Example

Which organisms return nutrients to the soil?

Bacteria and fungi

Answer: decomposers

Example

Producers have 10,000 kJ. About how much reaches the herbivores?

About 10%

Answer: 1,000 kJ

Common mistakes

  • Thinking energy is recycled like nutrients.
  • Drawing arrows from the eater to the eaten.
  • Thinking decomposers are not part of the food web.

faq.q: Why is the Sahel savanna at risk?
faq.a: Low rainfall, overgrazing and cutting down trees turn the land into desert (desertification).

faq.q: Why are there few top predators in an ecosystem?
faq.a: Little energy reaches the top of the food chain.

items.q: What is primary succession?
c: the arrival of predators in a new area
colonisation of bare rock or new land where there was no soil
regrowth of a forest after a bushfire
items.e: Lichens and mosses are pioneer species.

items.q: A tick feeds on the blood of a bandicoot. What is this relationship?
items.e: The parasite benefits and the host is harmed.

items.q: What is secondary succession?
c: a food chain with two consumers
regrowth of a community where soil remains after a disturbance such as fire
items.e: It is faster because soil and seeds are already there.

items.q: A new volcanic island rises from the sea. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: What is a pioneer species?
c: the largest tree in a forest
the first organism to colonise bare ground, such as lichen
items.e: Pioneers start to form soil.

items.q: A predator–prey graph shows the predator population peaking after the prey population. Why?
c: the two populations are not linked
predators increase only after there is plenty of prey, then fall when prey run short
items.e: The cycles are linked but out of step.

items.q: A population of 840 antelope has 37 births, 22 immigrants, 10 deaths and 29 emigrants in a year. What is the population at the end of the year?
items.e: Nt+1 = Nt + (B + I) − (D + E) = 860.

items.q: Which factor is density-independent?
c: disease spreading through a crowded colony
predation that increases with prey numbers
items.e: Drought affects a population whatever its density.

items.q: A remora fish attaches to a shark and eats scraps of its food; the shark is not affected. What is this relationship?
items.e: One benefits, the other is unaffected.

items.q: What is a keystone species?
c: the most common species in an ecosystem
a species whose effect on its ecosystem is much larger than its numbers suggest
the largest species in a food web
a species found only in one place
items.e: Removing it changes the whole community.

items.q: What is the carrying capacity of an environment?
c: the fastest rate at which a population can grow
the largest population it can support for a long time
the number of species it contains
items.e: Limited by food, water, space and other resources.

items.q: A forest fire burns trees but leaves the soil. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Which interaction is shown when a lyrebird and a bandicoot both dig in the leaf litter for the same insects?
items.e: Two species use the same limited resource.

items.q: What is an ecological niche?
c: the number of individuals of a species
the place where a species lives only
the role of a species, including what it eats, where it lives and how it interacts with others
the food chain a species belongs to
items.e: The habitat is only part of the niche.

items.q: Clownfish shelter in sea anemones and keep them clean; the anemone's stinging cells protect the fish. What is this relationship?
items.e: Both species benefit.

items.q: A glacier melts back and leaves bare rock. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: Lava cools into new bare rock. Lichens grow first. Which kind of succession follows?
items.e: Primary starts with no soil; secondary starts where soil remains.

items.q: A population of 260 antelope has 55 births, 10 immigrants, 37 deaths and 27 emigrants in a year. What is the population at the end of the year?
items.e: Nt+1 = Nt + (B + I) − (D + E) = 261.

items.q: Reef-building corals and the algae (zooxanthellae) in their tissues both benefit. What is this relationship?
items.e: The algae give sugars; the coral gives shelter and nutrients.

items.q: Mistletoe takes water and minerals from a eucalyptus. What is the mistletoe?
items.e: Mistletoes are partial parasites of trees.

items.q: The grass capture 10,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the mice?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 2 steps.

items.q: The grass capture 1,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the mice?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 2 steps.

items.q: Usman's energy pyramid shows 50,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 50,000 → 5,000.

items.q: Why are there few tuna compared with phytoplankton?
c: Little energy reaches the top of the pyramid.
items.e: Less energy supports fewer animals.

items.q: Nkechi's energy pyramid shows 5,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 5,000 → 500 → 50 → 5.

items.q: Tobi's energy pyramid shows 1,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 1,000 → 100.

items.q: Food chain: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → tuna. What trophic level are the phytoplankton?
items.e: Count from the producer.

items.q: The phytoplankton capture 100,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the zooplankton?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 1 step.

items.q: Why are there few snakes compared with grass?
c: Little energy reaches the top of the pyramid.
items.e: Less energy supports fewer animals.

items.q: Where does most of the energy at each level go?
c: It is recycled back to the producers.
It is lost as heat from respiration and in waste.
It stays stored forever in the top level.
items.e: About 90% is used or lost each step.

items.q: Chioma's energy pyramid shows 10,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 10,000 → 1,000.

items.q: Use the 10% rule. How much energy reaches the snakes?
The grass capture 5,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the grasshoppers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 1 step.

items.q: Use the 10% rule. How much energy reaches the tuna?
Nonso's energy pyramid shows 10,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100.

items.q: Hauwa's energy pyramid shows 2,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2,000 → 200 → 20.

items.q: Hadiza's energy pyramid shows 1,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 1,000 → 100 → 10 → 1.

items.q: The grass capture 100,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the snakes?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each step: 3 steps.

items.q: What percent of the energy at one level passes to the next level?
Hadiza's energy pyramid shows 2,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the primary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2,000 → 200.

items.q: Which pyramid can never be inverted?
items.e: Energy always decreases up the levels.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 3,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 3,000 × 0.13 = 3.00 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 40 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 40 × 10³ = 40,000 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 6,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 6,000 × 0.12 = 60.0 J.

items.q: A single eucalyptus supports thousands of caterpillars. What shape is the pyramid of numbers?
c: inverted at the base (one producer, many consumers)
items.e: Pyramids of numbers can be inverted; pyramids of energy cannot.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 10,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 10,000 × 0.13 = 10.0 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 70 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 70 × 10³ = 70,000 J.

items.q: Which process returns nutrients from dead organisms to the soil?
items.e: Decomposers recycle matter, not energy.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 20 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 20 × 10³ = 20,000 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 2,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 2,000 × 0.13 = 2.00 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 60,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 60,000 × 0.13 = 60.0 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 60 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 60 × 10³ = 60,000 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 4,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 4,000 × 0.12 = 40.0 J.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 30 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 30 × 10³ = 30,000 J.

items.q: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five links?
c: there is too much biomass at the top
too little energy is left at the top to support another level
plants cannot support more than one consumer
items.e: Energy decreases at each trophic level.

items.q: Tertiary consumers in a food chain receive 10 J. Using the 10% law, how much energy did the producers fix?
items.e: Go back three levels: 10 × 10³ = 10,000 J.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 80,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 80,000 × 0.12 = 800 J.

items.q: What is a trophic level?
c: a feeding position in a food chain
the number of organisms in a habitat
items.e: Producers are level 1, herbivores level 2.

items.q: Producers in a food chain fix 300,000 J of energy. Using the 10% law, how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Only about 10% passes to each level: 300,000 × 0.13 = 300 J.

items.q: The producers contain 8,000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and the primary consumers contain 960 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
items.e: Efficiency = energy at next level ÷ energy at previous level × 100 = 12.0%.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A rabbit eats the grass. Then the rabbit releases the carbon as CO<sub>2</sub>. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Nonso observes: “A fox breathes out carbon dioxide.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Tolu observes: “A leaf falls and decomposers break it down.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nutrients return to the soil for plants to use again.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Chidi observes: “Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Carbon from the air dissolves into the ocean. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Which processes return carbon to the air?
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Where do the atoms in your body come from?
c: from the food you eat, which came from plants and the air
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A carbon atom in CO<sub>2</sub> enters a grass leaf. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. A dead tree's carbon is released by fungi. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Which process puts carbon from the air into living things?
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Victor observes: “A rabbit eats grass.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Matter and energy in the grass move into the rabbit.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Where does decomposition move carbon?
c: from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere
from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
items.e: Decomposition moves carbon from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from producers into consumers?
items.e: Animals eating plants.

items.q: Where does animals eating plants move carbon?
c: from the hydrosphere into the geosphere
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
items.e: Animals eating plants moves carbon from producers into consumers.

items.q: Which process moves carbon from the geosphere into the atmosphere?
items.e: Burning fossil fuels.

items.q: In a swamp with little oxygen, how do some bacteria break down matter?
c: anaerobic respiration, which can release methane
they cannot break it down at all
items.e: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.

items.q: Where does formation of fossil fuels over millions of years move carbon?
c: from the atmosphere into living things
from the geosphere into the atmosphere
from dead organisms into the atmosphere and soil
from dead organisms into the geosphere
items.e: Formation of fossil fuels over millions of years moves carbon from dead organisms into the geosphere.

items.q: Segun observes: “A dead tree rots on the forest floor.” What does this show about matter in the ecosystem?
c: Carbon goes back into the air, where plants can take it in.
Carbon from the air becomes part of the plant.
Decomposers return carbon and nutrients to the air and soil.
Nitrogen cycles from the soil into plants.
items.e: Matter cycles among living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Carbon in coal returns to the air at a power station. Which process?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: Trace a carbon atom. Plankton remains are buried and pressed for millions of years. What forms?
items.e: Each step moves carbon to a new reservoir.

items.q: What is the shape of the pyramid of numbers in a grassland?
items.e: The pyramid of numbers in a grassland: upright.

items.q: What is the shape of the pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem?
items.e: The pyramid of numbers in a tree ecosystem: spindle-shaped (inverted in part).
